paragraphs.text: Lesson 32, common interjections.
Every day spoken English contains lots of little expressions, like,
wow, oops, aww, ooh, huh?
Oh, and cool.
Each of these interjections serves to express a particular emotion or attitude.
Listen to the conversation and then try the quick quiz to identify the function of each
of the ex-clamations in the dialogue.
Hey Laura, how are your kids doing these days?
Really well.
Eric's doing great in school and Kevin just got a full scholarship to university.
Wow, good for him.
What school?
Colgate University, his first choice was Middlebury College, but he actually missed the application
deadline.
Oops.
So, how are you feeling about Kevin going off to college?
Well, you know, this is a natural part of him growing up and he's ready, but I'll definitely
miss him at home.
Aww.
So what's new with you?
Don't you have a trip coming up?
Yeah, my company is sending me to India for a three month assignment.
Oh, how exciting.
When do you leave?
In about two weeks, but I don't have a place to stay when I get there so I'm desperately
trying to find one.
Huh?
Shouldn't the company have arranged that for you?
Well, they did, but it was a luxury apartment and the rent was being deducted from my salary,
so I told them I'd rather find my own place.
Oh, what are you doing there, work-wise?
Giving training seminars for the local staff, helping them develop their customer service
center?
What else?
Probably giving some English classes too.
Cool.
I hope you have a great time.
Be sure to post lots of pictures.
I will.
Now pause the audio to take the quick quiz where you try to identify the function of each
interjection in the conversation, then come back to the audio to hear the explanation.
How did you do?
Were you able to figure out what the words mean from the context of the conversation?
Here are a number of common interjections in English with their meanings and examples
of how to use them.
Aha.
Use aha when you suddenly make a discovery or find out some information that you had wanted
to know.
For example, the remote control's not working.
I wonder why.
Aha.
There aren't any batteries in it.
The interjections aha, oh, huh, and okay can all be used to say I understand, to show that
you're listening to what the other person is saying.
Note that, huh, used in this way, is different from, huh, which you'll learn later in this
lesson.
Here are some examples.
Sorry, you can't register for the new course.
The deadline has passed.
Oh, could you tell me when the next course will start?
Huh, is usually used for mild surprise.
For example, did you know that technically tomatoes are fruits?
Huh, I always thought of them as vegetables.
Aha.
Aha is used both to show sentimental approval.
For example, aha, what a cute puppy.
And to say, that's too bad.
For example, if your friend comments that his son lost his favorite toy, you could say, aww,
I'm sure he was sad about that.
Aha, aha, and oh.
These expressions are used at the beginning of a sentence to express mild protest.
For example, I'm not so sure I want to go water skiing.
Aww, it'll be fun.
Everyone else is going.
Guys, I think we should turn the music down.
It might bother the neighbors.
Oh, don't be such a party pooper.
It's not even that late.
A party pooper is someone who doesn't want other people to have fun.
Boo.
This is used to express disapproval.
People also yell boo at sports games to express their disapproval of the other team, or of a
player's mistake.
For example, I can't go on the trip this weekend.
I have to work.
Boo, I really wish you could go.
Burr.
This expression means it's cold.
For example, it's 5 degrees below zero outside.
Burr.
Drat.
And rats.
These expressions express disappointment and annoyance.
They are milder and more innocent forms of words like damn or crap.
For example, oh, drat.
I just deleted an important file by accident.
Rats is usually used in response to something disappointing.
For example, by the time I went to the supermarket, it was already closed.
Rats.
Well, I guess we'll have to wait till tomorrow to do the shopping.
Duh.
Duh is a sarcastic expression.
That means that's obvious and you're stupid for not realizing it.
It's rather rude.
For example, I just bought this computer and it won't even turn on.
You need to plug it in.
Duh.
When used in response to another person's statement, huh?
Expresses confusion as in the conversation between Connie and Laura.
When used at the end of your own statement, then it functions as a question tag.
For example, this line is really long.
I guess we'll be waiting for a while, huh?
Huh?
At the end means won't we or isn't that right?
Hm.
Um.
And uhh.
All of these are used for pausing and hesitating.
Hm.
Is the most pensive, for topics that you really do need to think about a little before responding.
Um.
And uhh.
Are quicker and more casual.
For example, if you could go back in time, what would you do differently?
Hm.
I probably would have studied harder in school.
I didn't really pay attention in any of my classes.
Excuse me.
Is there a bus stop around here?
Uhh.
I think there's one on 42nd street.
Hooray.
breh.
Hooray.
Hazah.
Woo hoo.
Yay.
These are all used for celebrating and expressing happiness.
For example, woo hoo, I just got free tickets to a World Cup game.
You can also use them in response to someone else's statement.
For example, the boss says we can all leave work early today.
Yay.
Ick.
Yuck.
Eww.
Pu.
pew.
Use these words to express disgust.
The expression pew is specifically used for disgusting smells.
For example, pew, something in the refrigerator really stinks.
Oh look, it's some rotting meat.
Yuck!
That must have been in there for months.
It's already turning green.
Meh.
And eh.
These expressions show indifference when you don't care or don't have a strong opinion about
something.
For example, where do you want to go for dinner?
There's a Japanese restaurant and a Mexican restaurant in this area.
Eh, anything's fine with me.
It's up to you.
That means you decide.
Ooh.
As you saw in the dialogue, ooh, can express interest or admiration.
Depending on the context, it can also mean that's bad.
It depends on how you say it.
For example, my brother and I went mountain biking for the first time last weekend.
Ooh, how was it?
Well, I loved it, but he crashed into a tree and broke his arm.
Ooh, that must have hurt.
Oops.
And, whoops.
Use these expressions in response to a small accident or small mistake.
For example, oops, I sent the email without the attachment.
Here's the file you need.
Oops, can also be pronounced oops, and ouch.
We say these when we get hurt.
For example, ow, I just slammed my finger in the door.
You can also use ouch as a casual response to a description of a situation that hurt someone
else.
For example, Sally's boyfriend broke up with her on her birthday.
Ouch, that was pretty mean.
These sounds are used to say, that's nothing.
To express the fact that you are not impressed.
They are rather sarcastic and rude.
For example, I can run a mile in eight minutes.
I can run a mile in six minutes.
Phew, and whew.
These are also more of a sound than an actual word.
Use them to express relief.
For example, I hadn't studied for the test at all, but then I found out that the teacher
moved it to next week.
Whew, now I have more time to prepare.
We use this sound to get someone's attention when we want to whisper or speak to them very
quietly.
For example, pst, your fly is unzipped.
The fly is the zipper on your pants or jeans.
Sheesh and geez.
These exclamations express exasperation or annoyance.
For example, I was on the phone for two hours, but I still couldn't resolve the problem with
my credit card bill.
Geez, that's ridiculous.
You'd think such a big company would provide better customer service.
Shh, and shush.
These sounds are used to tell someone to be quiet.
Shh is gentler than shush.
For example, shh, the movie's starting.
I can say this when the film is about to start and I want to tell people to stop talking.
Shh, this is an informal expression used to tell children or animals to go away.
For example, the dogs always come in the kitchen when I'm cooking.
Shh, uh oh, and oh no.
These expressions show concern about something bad that has happened or is happening.
For example, oh no, we don't have any milk.
Or that might or will happen in the future.
For example, uh oh, the weather forecast says it's going to rain this weekend.
The festival's probably going to be cancelled.
Wow, woah, and yikes.
All of these words express surprise.
Wow can be used for good or bad surprises.
Yikes is more typically used for neutral or bad surprises and woah can also be used for
disbelief.
For example, I'm planning to hike across the United States.
Yikes, that's quite a long distance.
It's going to cost $300 to change the flight.
Woah, are you sure?
On the airlines website it says the fee is $150.
You've finished lesson 32.
Now take the quiz to see how well you learned the different interjections.
Choose the best response for each situation.
